questions.q: What three things determine what you get out of an hour?
a: What you do, how much energy you have and how present you are
Your income, your schedule and your willpower
The time of day, your age and your mood
How busy you are, how much you finish and how fast you work
questions.why: Lesson 1 says an hour's value depends on how you spend it, your energy and your mindfulness.

questions.q: What does the summary say about an hour spent scrolling on your phone?
a: It is worth much less than an hour of meaningful or pleasurable activity
It restores energy better than rest or sleep
It counts the same as any other hour
It improves focus for the next task
questions.why: Lesson 1 contrasts useful, pleasurable hours with time lost to surfing the internet.

questions.q: In the garden metaphor, what do time, energy and attention represent?
a: The water you use to nourish your plants
The seeds you choose to plant
The soil that holds everything together
The fence that keeps pests out
questions.why: Lesson 2 compares your resources to water, which is limited and must be shared among the plants.

questions.q: What risk does the summary warn about when you overwater one plant?
a: Other areas of your life wither because resources are limited
The garden grows faster than you can manage
The plant stops producing fruit entirely
Weeds spread to the neighbouring plots
questions.why: Lesson 2 says pouring too much into one area, such as work, can kill your relationships and health.

questions.q: What does the summary say is the key to slowing time down?
a: Putting away distractions and concentrating fully on the experience
Scheduling fewer activities each day
Sleeping more hours each night
Measuring how long each task takes
questions.why: Lesson 3 says mindfulness, focusing on the moment, makes experiences register and time feel slower.
